title: The Image of the City
authority: Kevin Lynch was an MIT urban planner whose five-year study of Boston, Jersey City and Los Angeles founded the field of environmental legibility and mental-map research.
caveats: Small interview samples (about 30 Boston residents, mostly professionals); later work (Passini, Golledge) shows individual and cultural variation and that maps are not purely imageable by form. Findings concern physical cities; transfer to screens is by analogy.

title: Cognitive maps in rats and men
authority: Tolman was a leading behaviorist-era psychologist at Berkeley; this paper introduced the term cognitive map.
caveats: Rat maze evidence was contested at the time and later reinterpreted (O'Keefe and Nadel 1978 place cells support map-like representations); human claims are speculative in this paper.

title: Wayfinding in Architecture
authority: Passini was a professor at the University of Montreal and the founder of the behavioral, problem-solving view of wayfinding.
caveats: Based on building case studies and think-aloud protocols with small samples; qualitative.

title: Wayfinding: People, Signs, and Architecture
authority: Arthur is a Canadian graphic designer who designed signage programs; Passini is the leading wayfinding researcher. The book is the standard practitioner text on signage programs.
caveats: Practitioner synthesis; empirical support is largely case-based. Not verified by search this session.

title: Wayshowing: A Guide to Environmental Signage Principles and Practices
authority: Mollerup is a Danish-Australian design professor who systematised wayshowing principles and wrote on signage and design theory.
caveats: Practitioner and theoretical synthesis rather than experimental evidence. Revised as Wayshowing > Wayfinding (BIS, 2013).

title: Information foraging
authority: Pirolli and Card were Xerox PARC researchers; the paper introduced information foraging theory, drawing on optimal foraging theory and the ACT-R architecture.
caveats: Model validated mainly on Scatter/Gather and similar tasks with small user studies; ACT-IF simulations are fitted, not broadly replicated. Later work (Pirolli 2007 book) extends it. Nielsen's popularisation simplified it.

title: Using information scent to model user information needs and actions on the Web
authority: Xerox PARC authors who operationalised information scent as a computable measure from text similarity and usage data (the Bloodhound / Inferring User Need by Information Scent, IUNIS, algorithm).
caveats: Evaluated on a few sites with web-log data; predictions are approximate.

title: Web page design: implications of memory, structure and scent for information retrieval
authority: Microsoft Research usability researchers; one of the first web studies of breadth versus depth with scent as a factor.
caveats: Abstract confirmed: increased depth harmed web search performance, but a medium balance of depth and breadth outperformed the broadest shallow structure overall. Sample size and the exact structures and percentages were not confirmed this session and are not asserted in the notes. Label ambiguity (scent) was a studied factor.

title: The depth/breadth tradeoff in hierarchical computer menus
container: Proceedings of the Human Factors Society 25th Annual Meeting
authority: Cited in the menu-design literature as an early empirical study of depth versus breadth in hierarchical computer menus. Not independently confirmed this session: web search budget ran out before it could be checked.
caveats: Existence, pages and the specific conditions tested were not confirmed by search this session. Secondary sources report only that Miller's work is cited as a short-term-memory-based argument about menu depth. Treat any specific numbers attributed to it as unverified.

title: The depth/breadth trade-off in the design of menu-driven user interfaces
authority: Peer-reviewed study in the International Journal of Man-Machine Studies (volume 20, pages 201-213, confirmed by a citation in a usability report); widely cited as showing that broader, shallower menus outperform deeper ones.
caveats: Only the citation was confirmed this session. The specific structures tested and numeric results are recalled from secondary descriptions and not confirmed. Early text-menu interface; results depend on how well items are categorised.

title: Depth vs breadth in the arrangement of web links
container: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
authority: Zaphiris studied web link hierarchies at the University of Maryland HCIL and later at City University London; this paper tested depth against breadth in web links.
caveats: Search confirmed a Zaphiris 2000 paper titled 'Depth vs breadth in the arrangement of web links' exists (full text hosted by Cyprus University of Technology); volume and pages not confirmed so left empty. Related: Zaphiris, Shneiderman and Norman 2002, Behaviour and Information Technology, on expandable indexes versus sequential menus.

title: The vocabulary problem in human-system communication
authority: Bell Labs and Bellcore researchers; empirical demonstration that people rarely choose the same word for the same thing.
caveats: Based on 1980s command and object-naming tasks; the core result has repeatedly been echoed in search-query studies.

title: The design of browsing and berrypicking techniques for the online search interface
authority: Bates is a UCLA information science professor; the berrypicking model is among the most cited models of real information seeking.
caveats: Conceptual model derived from observed searches and the literature; not an experiment.

title: Exploratory search: from finding to understanding
authority: Marchionini is a UNC information scientist; this paper defines lookup, learn and investigate search activities.
caveats: Conceptual framework with few empirical numbers.

title: Information Architecture: For the Web and Beyond
edition: 4th ed., 2015 (first ed. 1998 titled Information Architecture for the World Wide Web)
authority: The field-defining practitioner text, by the co-founders of the Argus Associates practice and the Information Architecture Institute.
caveats: Practitioner synthesis; guidelines are experience-based. Page-level details varied between editions.

title: A Practical Guide to Information Architecture
authority: Spencer is an established Australian IA practitioner who also wrote Card Sorting (Rosenfeld Media, 2009).
caveats: Practitioner guidance. Card sort sample sizes: Tullis and Wood (2004) is the usual source for 'about 15 to 30' participants; their exact correlation figures were not confirmed this session.

title: Information Anxiety
authority: Wurman, architect and founder of TED, coined 'information architect' and proposed the LATCH organising principles.
caveats: Essayistic and non-empirical; LATCH is a useful taxonomy but not experimentally validated.
